opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question we've been thinking about quite a lot, because it really goes to the heart of what we mean when we say we want to treat neural network weights as a data modality in their own right.

When we started working on what we call hyper-representations, the idea was to take populations of trained models, what we call model zoos, and learn representations directly over their weights. Initially we looked at full model weights, the entire parameter vector of a network. That's appealing because it's the complete description of the model: if you can learn the distribution over full weights, you can in principle generate entirely new models from scratch, sample initializations that train faster, or predict properties like accuracy or generalization gap just by looking at the parameters.

But full weights come with real challenges. They're very high-dimensional, and they carry many symmetries, like permutation symmetries of neurons and scaling symmetries, that have nothing to do with what the model actually does. So a lot of the learning effort goes into dealing with structure that's irrelevant. And as models get bigger, especially in the foundation-model era, it becomes impractical to learn over billions of parameters directly.

That's where task vectors become interesting. A task vector is the difference between a fine-tuned model and its pre-trained base. So you're no longer modeling the whole network, you're modeling the *change* that encodes a specific capability or task. It's a much more focused signal. Because everything is anchored to a shared pre-trained model, many of the symmetry problems are reduced. All the fine-tuned models live in roughly the same basin, so the deltas are comparable in a way that weights from independently trained models aren't.

Practically, that changes how I think about the targets. Full weights are the right target when you care about the model population as a whole: understanding training dynamics, generating initializations, studying how architectures and hyperparameters shape the weight space. Task vectors, or other parameter-efficient deltas like LoRA adapters, are the right target when you live in a world of large pre-trained backbones and want to reason about skills: generating an adapter for a new task, combining or editing capabilities, or predicting how a fine-tune will behave before you even run it.

I see them as two levels of the same idea. Full weights are like learning over the whole organism; task vectors are like learning over the specific adaptations. Going forward, given where the field is, I think the more scalable and maybe more useful direction is learning over these deltas, because that's where the variation that matters actually sits. But the lessons we learned from full-weight model zoos, about symmetries, about what structure in weight space is meaningful, carry over directly. In a sense, the full-weight work was necessary groundwork to understand what makes weight space learnable at all.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we've been thinking about a lot, because it really changes what the object of learning is. When we started this line of work on hypernetworks and generating weights, the first instinct is always to go for the full model weights. You take a model zoo, a population of trained networks, and you try to learn a representation of the entire parameter space. And you can do that, we've done it, we trained hyper-representations over thousands of small models and generated new ones from that latent space. But the problem is that full weights carry an enormous amount of information that has nothing to do with the task. You have the initialization, you have the training trajectory, the random seed, all of these permutation symmetries in the layers, and most of that is noise from the perspective of what the model actually learned to do.

Task vectors are interesting precisely because they factor that out. You take the fine-tuned weights, you subtract the pre-trained base, and what remains is in some sense the delta that encodes the adaptation to the task. And what's remarkable is how structured that delta is. It lives in a much lower dimensional subspace, it's often quite sparse, and you can do arithmetic on it. You can add task vectors to compose skills, you can negate them to unlearn things, you can interpolate between them. That arithmetic property is a strong hint that this is a much better coordinate system for learning and generation than the raw weight space.

So the way I think about it now is that the pre-trained model gives you a shared anchor, a common origin, and task vectors are displacements from that origin. If you want to learn a generative model over models, you want to generate in that displacement space, not in the absolute space. The distribution is tighter, it's more semantically meaningful, and the samples you draw are much more likely to be functional, because you're always starting from something that already works and moving in a direction that has meaning. With full weights, if you sample a bit off manifold, you get a model that does nothing. With task vectors, you're sampling a direction of adaptation, and even a slightly off sample tends to degrade gracefully rather than collapse.

There are caveats of course. Task vectors are only comparable when they come from the same base model, so you lose some generality compared to approaches that try to learn across architectures. And with things like LoRA you're already working with a parameterized low-rank version of the task vector, which is convenient, but it also imposes a prior that may or may not match what the task actually needs. But if the question is where I'd place my bets for learning over populations of models and generating new ones, it's clearly on the task vector side. The full weights are the substrate. The task vectors are where the knowledge is.

r001.rationale: The response argues that task vectors are a better coordinate system for learning, but does not say their relative ease of learning varies across experimental setups.

r002.rationale: The response favors generating in task-vector space, but does not state that the relative ease of generation varies across setups.

r003.rationale: The response gives reasons for preferring task vectors and notes caveats, but does not say Damian Borth and his collaborators cannot explain why different setups favor different targets.

astra-6.text:
I think the important distinction is whether you want to learn the model itself or the change that makes a model useful for a particular task. If you start from a pretrained model and fine-tune it, the task vector is simply the difference between those two sets of weights. So you’re describing a transformation relative to a shared starting point.

That’s an attractive target for learning or generation because the pretrained model already contains a lot of capability. You don’t necessarily want to regenerate all of that. You want to capture what needs to change to adapt it. And with a common starting point, you can investigate whether those changes can be combined, scaled, or transferred across tasks.

But a task vector isn’t automatically a compact representation. It can have exactly as many entries as the full model, and its meaning depends on the base model. A change learned from one initialization is not necessarily meaningful when applied to another.

With full model weights, you’re asking a broader question: can we learn a distribution over networks and generate an entire network from it? That brings in challenges like weight symmetries—different weight configurations can implement the same function. So I see these as related targets with different assumptions. Task vectors give you a shared reference point and let you focus on adaptation. Full-weight generation asks you to capture much more of the structure of the model itself.

r001.rationale: It contrasts task vectors with full weights, but does not state that which is easier to learn depends on the experimental setup.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning or generating both targets, but does not say their relative ease of generation varies across setups.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Damian Borth and his collaborators being unable to explain why different setups favor different targets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the task vector is often the more interesting object to learn. If you start with a pretrained model and fine-tune it for a particular task, you can take the difference between those two sets of weights. That difference is the task vector. So instead of asking, “Can I generate an entire neural network?” you ask, “Can I generate the change that gives this network a particular capability?”

That gives you a shared reference point. If several models were fine-tuned from the same initialization, their task vectors describe different adaptations of the same underlying model. You can then study whether those adaptations can be combined, interpolated, or generated for a new task.

But there’s an important qualification: the task vector still has the same number of parameters as the model. Taking a difference doesn’t automatically make the learning problem small. You still need to find structure, perhaps through a lower-dimensional representation. And those vectors depend on the base model; you can’t assume a vector learned for one model will transfer directly to another.

So I see full-weight generation as the broader ambition, while task-vector generation gives us a more constrained question: given what the pretrained model already knows, what needs to change?
